title: Back to the brick
hook: Kids are moving to screens. How far do you take the brick?

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: Money LEGO has to pay its bills

future.label: Future
future.hint: How strong LEGO will be in the years ahead

intro.text: It is 1998. For about 50 years, children have built with your plastic bricks. You run LEGOLAND parks in Denmark and England, and in 1996 you started a team to make computer games. But kids now love game consoles, and this year, for the first time in its history, LEGO loses money.

d1.title: Beyond the brick
d1.setup: Since 1993 your sales have hardly grown. You keep adding new toys, but you are not selling more of them. Now you can make Star Wars sets. Some of your team also want more parks, more games, clothes and many new products.
d1.question: How do you grow LEGO?
d1.advisor: Kids still love to build. The question is how far from the brick you can go.

options.label: Go big: Star Wars sets, new parks, games, clothes and many new toys.
options.outcome: In 1999 LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets. They sold so well that LEGO made a profit again that year. LEGOLAND California opened too. LEGO also moved into electronics, video games, jewellery and learning centres, and it had three times as many products as before. But in 2000 LEGO lost 831 million kroner. It cut 1,500 jobs and stopped making clothes, watches and books.
options.why: Star Wars was a smart bet, because it still sold bricks. But parks, clothes and watches pulled money and attention away from the brick, and too many products made everything cost more.
options.better: Take the Star Wars deal, because it sells bricks, but say no to side businesses that are not built from the brick.
options.takeaway: In 1999 you grew in every direction at once. Some bets sold bricks; many just added cost.

options.label: Make Star Wars sets, but only brick sets. Say no to clothes and side businesses.
options.outcome: Our estimate: Star Wars sets bring new fans to the brick. With fewer side businesses, your money and your best people stay on the toy kids love most, and costs stay under control.
options.why: You used a popular story to sell more of what you do best, and you did not spread yourself thin.
options.takeaway: In 1999 you grew through the brick, not away from it.

options.label: Say no to films and screens. Keep making classic brick sets as they are.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you keep things simple, but you miss the Star Wars boom. Kids who love films and games walk past your sets, and sales keep slipping.
options.why: Kids' lives were changing. Ignoring that change does not protect the brick; it makes the brick look old.
options.better: Use popular stories like Star Wars to bring kids to the brick, while staying careful about side businesses.
options.takeaway: In 1999 you ignored how kids were changing. Standing still is also a risky bet.

d2.title: New toys for a new age

setup.text: Our estimate: it is 2002. Without film sets, your sales are flat. Your own new line, Bionicle, sells well: heroes you build from LEGO parts, with their own story. Your team wants to move further from the brick.

It is 2002. Your Star Wars and Harry Potter sets sell very well, but only in years when a new film comes out. Your own new line, Bionicle, is a hit: heroes you build from LEGO parts, with their own story. Your team wants to move further from the brick.

d2.question: Which new toys do you bet on?
d2.advisor: Every new toy should answer one question: does it make kids want to build?

options.label: Replace DUPLO in America with Explore toys, and launch Galidor action figures with a TV show.
options.outcome: In 2002 LEGO replaced DUPLO, its big bricks for small children, with a new brand called Explore in the United States. Parents did not see Explore as LEGO, and it did not sell. It cost about 500 million kroner. LEGO also launched Galidor, action figures with special parts and a TV show that LEGO paid for. The show was not popular, and the toys sold badly.
options.why: You swapped a brand parents trusted for one they did not know, and you made toys that were hardly LEGO at all. Both moved you away from the brick.
options.better: Grow from the brick, like Bionicle did: new stories and new shapes, but always built from parts that fit with other LEGO parts.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you moved away from what customers loved, and they stopped buying.

options.label: Cut prices on your sets to keep sales up between films.
options.outcome: Our estimate: shops sell more boxes, but each one makes less money. The real problem, too many costly products, stays hidden.
options.why: Lower prices bought some sales, but they did not fix what was wrong with the product range.
options.better: Fix the range first: fewer, better sets built from the brick, and stories like Bionicle that sell every year.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you used discounts to hide a product problem.

options.label: Make more lines like Bionicle: new stories, always built from LEGO parts.
options.outcome: Our estimate: lines like Bionicle give kids a reason to buy every year, not just in film years. DUPLO keeps its place with small children, and parents keep trusting the name.
options.why: You found something that worked and did more of it, without leaving the brick behind.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you built new ideas on top of your strongest asset.

text.text: It is 2004. In 2003 LEGO lost about 1.4 billion kroner before tax, the biggest loss in its history. The company is almost out of cash and owes nearly $1 billion. Some sets have parts that cost more to make than the whole box sells for, and nobody knows which products make money. The owner family puts 800 million kroner of its own money in, and a new CEO takes over. That CEO is you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. Explore and Galidor have flopped, and money is running out. The board brings in a new CEO to save the company. That CEO is you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. Sales have been weak for years, and money is tight. The board wants a new plan, and it wants it from you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. LEGO is in better shape than many toy makers, but costs are high. The board wants a plan for the next ten years.

d3.title: Stop the bleeding

setup.text: LEGO owns four LEGOLAND parks, a video game company and a huge range of products. You need cash fast, and you need to stop the losses.
Our estimate: LEGO owns LEGOLAND parks, a video game team and many products it does not need. Costs are too high for the money coming in.

d3.question: Where do you start?
d3.advisor: Ask one thing about every business: does it help kids build with LEGO bricks?

options.label: Borrow more and keep everything. The next big film will bring sales back.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the bank lends you money, but the interest piles up. The parks and the games team keep eating cash, and the film you were waiting for does not come in time.
options.why: Borrowing to keep a broken business going only makes the hole deeper.
options.better: Sell what others can run better, close what loses money, and spend your cash on the brick.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you borrowed time instead of fixing the problem.

options.label: Sell the LEGOLAND parks, close the game company, bring back DUPLO and focus on the brick.

outcome.text: In 2004 LEGO cut about 1,000 jobs and closed its video game company. Some of its staff set up a new firm that published LEGO games made by an outside studio. Their LEGO Star Wars game came out in 2005 and sold 3.3 million copies by March 2006. DUPLO came back in 2004. In 2005 LEGO sold its four LEGOLAND parks to Merlin Entertainments, owned by Blackstone, for €375 million, and kept 30% of Merlin. The money helped LEGO fix its main business.
Our estimate: you sell the parks to a theme park company and keep a share. You close your game team and let a partner make LEGO games. The cash gives you room to fix the brick business.

options.why: You let go of businesses that did not need LEGO to own them, raised cash, and put all your effort back into the brick.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you sold what others could run better and went back to your core.

options.label: Cut jobs and costs everywhere, but keep the parks and the games.
options.outcome: Our estimate: costs fall for a while, but the parks still need big money and the games still lose it. LEGO is smaller, but not more focused.
options.why: Cutting a little from everything feels fair, but it keeps the parts that drain you.
options.better: Sell what others can run better, like theme parks, and let studios make LEGO games. Spend your cash on the brick.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you cut costs but kept the businesses that caused them.

d4.title: Too many pieces
d4.setup: LEGO makes about 13,000 different pieces. Every new piece costs money to design, make, store and ship, and many are used in only a few sets.
d4.question: What do you do with all these pieces?
d4.advisor: A good LEGO piece is one you can use in a hundred models, not one.

options.label: Cut the number of pieces by about half. Every new piece must earn its place.

outcome.text: LEGO cut the number of different pieces it made from about 13,000 to 6,000, and stopped making toys that did not sell. It put profit first and growth second. In 2005 LEGO made a profit of 505 million kroner, after losing 1.93 billion kroner in 2004. Sales grew 12% to 7.05 billion kroner, led by Bionicle, DUPLO, LEGO City and LEGO Star Wars.
Our estimate: with about half as many pieces, sets cost less to make and are easier to keep in stock. Designers get more creative inside clear limits, and profit starts to come back.

options.why: Fewer pieces meant lower costs everywhere, from the factory to the warehouse, and the old pieces could still build almost anything.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you cut the complexity that was quietly eating your profit.

options.label: Keep every piece. Designers need freedom to make new things.
options.outcome: Our estimate: designers stay happy, but costs stay high. Warehouses fill with pieces few sets need, and many boxes still lose money.
options.why: Freedom without limits made LEGO expensive to run. Every extra piece had a cost that nobody was counting.
options.better: Cut the list of pieces and make each new one prove it will be used in many sets.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you kept the hidden costs that had nearly sunk LEGO.

options.label: Make fewer sets, but keep all the pieces in case you need them.
options.outcome: Our estimate: shops get a cleaner range, but the factory still has to handle thousands of pieces. Costs fall a little, not a lot.
options.why: It fixed what customers see, but not the costs hidden in the factory.
options.better: Cut the pieces too, not just the sets. That is where most of the cost hides.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you tidied the shelf but not the factory.

d5.title: Who makes the bricks?
d5.setup: LEGO is closing a factory in Switzerland and wants to make more bricks in countries where costs are lower. A big contract manufacturer called Flextronics offers to make many of your bricks for you.
d5.question: How do you make bricks for less?
d5.advisor: Your bricks must fit together perfectly, every time. Whoever makes them must care about that as much as you do.

options.label: Keep all your old factories as they are. Only LEGO can make LEGO.
options.outcome: Our estimate: quality stays perfect, but your costs stay far above other toy makers'. Each box earns less, and there is little money left for new ideas.
options.why: Pride in how you make things is good. But refusing to change where and how you make them leaves you too expensive.
options.better: Move making to cheaper places, but in factories you own and run yourself.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you protected old factories instead of the company.

options.label: Hand much of your brick making to Flextronics to save money.
options.outcome: From 2006 LEGO moved a large part of its making, especially DUPLO, to Flextronics plants in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Mexico. There were problems from the start. Parts ran short and LEGO could not make enough to meet demand; Flextronics could not even make enough DUPLO flowers. In 2008 LEGO ended the deal and took the work back. In 2009 it opened its own factories in Hungary and Mexico.
options.why: Cutting costs was right. But making perfect bricks was a core skill, and LEGO learned it could not hand that to someone else.
options.better: Move making to cheaper places, but in your own factories, run by your own people.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you outsourced a core skill, and had to take it back.

options.label: Run your own factories in cheaper countries, close to your buyers.
options.outcome: Our estimate: it takes longer and costs more at first, but you keep control of quality, and shops never run short of your sets.
options.why: You cut costs without giving away the skill that makes LEGO special.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you lowered costs but kept your core skill in your own hands.

text.text: LEGO kept growing. In the first half of 2014 its sales were more than three times what they were in the first half of 2008. The LEGO Movie came out in 2014 and earned about $500 million around the world, and that year LEGO passed Mattel, the maker of Barbie, in half-year sales. By 2015 LEGO was the biggest toy company in the world by sales. A company that almost ran out of cash in 2003 was now the leader.
Our estimate: you kept LEGO close to the brick and fixed problems early. LEGO grows year after year and becomes one of the most loved toy companies in the world.

survivor.title: Still building
survivor.text: Our estimate: LEGO survives and makes money again, but it is smaller and slower than it could have been. Other toy makers take the lead.

collapse.title: The brick breaks
collapse.text: Our estimate: the losses never stop. The owner family has to sell LEGO to a bigger toy company, and the brick becomes just one brand among many.

fired.title: The family lets you go
fired.text: Our estimate: three costly calls. The owner family loses trust in you and asks someone else to save LEGO.

realHistory: In the late 1990s LEGO grew far beyond the brick: theme parks, video games, clothes, electronics and toys like Explore and Galidor. In 2003 it lost about 1.4 billion kroner before tax, its biggest loss ever, and it was almost out of cash. A new CEO took over in 2004. LEGO closed its game company, sold its four LEGOLAND parks for €375 million, brought back DUPLO and cut its pieces from about 13,000 to 6,000. It made a profit again in 2005. A plan to let another company make its bricks failed, and LEGO took the work back in 2008. By 2015 LEGO was the biggest toy company in the world by sales.
